Reading 2 assumes the method succeeded and the record changed, reading 1 assumes the write was ignored and the original value stands, and reading a missing accessor complaint mistakes the illegal write for a missing method.
questions.hint: Every component of a record is fixed when the record is built.
questions.learningObjective: diagnose an attempt to write a component field of a record

options.misconception: believes a record component can be written after construction
options.text: It compiles and prints 2, because the component grew.

options.misconception: believes the compiler drops a write to a fixed component silently
options.text: It compiles and prints 1, ignoring the illegal write.

options.misconception: believes a record needs an accessor written out by hand
options.text: It fails to compile because the accessor is missing.
It fails to compile; a record component is final.

questions.topic: A Record Component Cannot Be Reassigned

questions.explanation: A record is a small class, so besides the accessor generated for the component it can hold ordinary methods, and here the accessor hands back 3 while the written method doubles that same component to 6, giving 3 6. Reading 6 6 assumes the accessor and the method return the same thing, and reading 3 3 assumes the extra method is never called.
questions.hint: The generated accessor and the written method both read the component.
questions.learningObjective: call a method written on a record beside its accessors

options.text: It prints 6 6, because both calls double the component.
It prints 3 6, from the accessor and the method.

options.misconception: believes a record may not carry methods of its own
options.text: It prints 3 3, because the extra method is ignored.

options.misconception: believes a record cannot declare a method beside its components
options.text: It fails to compile, since a record holds data only.

questions.topic: A Record Carries Behaviour Alongside Its Data

questions.explanation: A compact constructor is the place to validate what the components are about to hold, and with a row of 0 the condition holds and the exception is thrown before the record exists, so the catch block prints the message it carried. Reading 0 assumes the record was built and its component printed, and reading an escaping exception assumes nothing catches what the check throws.
questions.hint: The check runs before the component values are stored.

questions.topic: A Compact Constructor Can Check Its Parts

questions.explanation: A record may declare that it implements an interface as long as it supplies the operation the interface demands, and here the public rank method packs the row into the hundreds and the seat into the units, so 4 and 7 pack to 407 while 4 and 2 pack to 402, and the test of 407 above 402 is true. Reading false assumes the seat is packed into the more significant place, and reading 407 assumes the operation hands back its own number rather than a comparison of two of them.
questions.hint: The record supplies the operation and packs its components into a number.
questions.learningObjective: have a record supply the operation a plain interface demands

options.text: It prints 407, because the operation returns the packed value.

options.misconception: believes a record is barred from declaring an implemented interface

It prints true, because 407 sorts above 402.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: A Record Can Satisfy An Interface

questions.explanation: A record extends nothing, because the language extends the class it would otherwise need in order to hold its components, and naming a superclass is rejected by the compiler, while implementing interfaces is allowed. Reading a successful compile assumes a record behaves like any other class for inheritance, reading a null complaint mistakes the rule for a null field, and reading a private complaint confuses it with an access limit.
questions.hint: A record has no superclass to extend, only interfaces to implement.
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a record that tries to extend a class

options.text: It compiles and prints 1, the inherited field value.

options.misconception: believes a superclass has to be declared in a separate source file
options.text: It fails to compile because Base is in another file.

questions.explanation: A record may hold state only through the components listed in its header, and a separate instance field is not one of them, so the compiler rejects the declaration. Reading a successful run assumes any field may sit beside the components, reading 5 assumes the extra field is reported in the text form, and reading a missing accessor complaint mistakes the ban on extra state for a missing method.
questions.hint: The components are the only state a record may hold.

questions.topic: ARecord Cannot Declare An Extra Field

questions.explanation: A static method on a record lives on the record type itself, so calling it needs no instance and it builds a record whose component is 1, whose ordinary method then doubles that to 2, giving 2. Reading 1 assumes the static call returns the component rather than a record, and reading a failure assumes a static method on a record is treated as a component.
questions.hint: A static method belongs to the record type, not to any one record.

options.text: It fails to compile, as records allow no static methods.

options.misconception: believes an instance method reads the default when built by a factory
options.text: It prints 0, because a static call has no component.

questions.topic: A Static Method On A Record Is Not A Component

questions.explanation: Every constant of an enum is its own object, built once by the enum constructor with the argument written beside it, so SLOW holds a factor of 1 and FAST holds 5, and looking one up by name returns that same FAST object, which is why the name prints as SLOW, the field as 5, and the looked up field as 5. Reading 1 5 5 assumes the first constant is printed by its field, and reading SLOW 1 1 assumes every constant shares one field value.
questions.hint: Each constant is a distinct object built once by the enum constructor.
questions.learningObjective: read per constant fields built by an enum constructor

options.text: It prints 1 5 5, showing the first field rather than the name.

options.misconception: believes a field set by a constructor is shared by all the constants
options.text: It prints SLOW 1 1, sharing one field across constants.
It prints SLOW 5 5, since each constant has its own field.

options.misconception: believes looking up a constant by name alters the earlier constant
options.text: It prints FAST 5 5, because a lookup changes the first value.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Enum Constants Carry Their Own Fields

questions.explanation: A constant may carry a class body that supplies its own version of the shared step, so the loop over the constants calls the addition for the first and the multiplication for the second, which gives 7 and 12 in declaration order. Reading 12 7 assumes the loop visits the constants in reverse declaration order, and reading 7 7 assumes a constant without a body would fall back to some shared arithmetic that happens to add.
questions.hint: A constant with a body replaces the shared step for that constant only.
questions.learningObjective: run a shared abstract step that each enum constant implements

options.misconception: believes a constant body cannot replace the shared step
options.text: It prints 7 7, because every constant uses the same step.

options.misconception: believes the shared step and the constant body both run per call
options.text: It prints 7 12 7, once per body plus the shared step.
It prints 7 12, adding for the first and multiplying next.
